analysis.one_liner: Creates new federal crimes for public corruption, election fraud, and retaliating against whistleblowing government workers.
analysis.headline: The Senate's 1995 anti-corruption bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or a vote, and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have made it a federal crime, punishable by up to 10 years in prison, to cheat the public out of the honest services of a government official or out of a fair election — covering fraudulent ballots, paying people to vote, fake voter registrations, false campaign-finance reports, and intimidating voters. It would have criminalized officials firing, demoting, or harassing employees to hide a fraud scheme, and given those workers a court remedy including backpay and reinstatement. It also would have extended federal fraud law to any use of interstate commerce and created a serious felony for officials taking bribes in connection with illegal drugs. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced and never received any further action.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of states and towns whose officials defraud them or rig elections would get a federal criminal backstop; government employees who report or help prosecute corruption would get protection from retaliation, with reinstatement, backpay, double backpay as a penalty, and attorney's fees if they win in court.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it a federal crime carrying up to 10 years in prison to defraud the inhabitants of a state or the United States of the honest services of a government official, or of a fair and impartially conducted election [S2][S3].

The election-fraud offense covers false or fraudulent ballots, paying anyone to vote, false voter registrations, false campaign-finance reports, and intimidating or deceiving people to keep them from voting or campaigning [S3].

Officials who fire, demote, suspend, threaten, or harass employees in order to carry out or conceal a fraud scheme would face up to 5 years in prison, and the affected worker could sue for reinstatement, backpay, a penalty of two times backpay, and attorney's fees [S2][S3].

Extends the federal fraud statute to cover use of any facility of interstate or foreign commerce, and creates a class B felony for public officials who take anything of value to further or conceal drug trafficking [S2][S3].
The new corruption offenses would be added to the list of crimes for which prosecutors can seek wiretaps under existing federal law [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corrupt officials and anyone running election-fraud schemes would face federal prison terms; state and local governments would bear civil liability, and could in turn seek contribution from the individual employees whose conduct caused the judgment. Federal courts and prosecutors would take on more cases that today are handled by state authorities.

drawbacks.text: The bill federalizes conduct — local corruption and election administration — that states largely police themselves, and its honest-services language is broad and vague, the same kind of provision federal courts have struggled to define [S3].

A worker suing a state for the doubled-backpay penalty or special damages must prove the violations were 'widespread' or authorized by a senior official — a high bar that would leave many individually retaliated employees with a much weaker remedy [S3].
The bill's crimes mostly overlap with existing state bribery, election-fraud, and federal mail-fraud statutes, so its practical added benefit beyond stiffer penalties is unclear [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would give victims of official corruption and rigged elections a federal backstop and give whistleblowing employees real protection, which is a genuine public good. The costs are the risk of over-federalizing local matters, vague 'honest services' language inviting arbitrary prosecution, and a whistleblower remedy sharply limited against state governments. On balance it is a good-faith anti-corruption measure, though one whose scope a careful legislature would likely have narrowed in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, got no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsors, and died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell introduced the bill on November 2, 1995; it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1][S5].
The action history shows no further steps — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent officials and state and local governments, who face no new federal criminal exposure or civil liability from this bill; corrupt conduct remains policed only under existing state and federal law.

for.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kentucky; bill sponsor

against.name: Sen. Orrin Hatch
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee without action until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsors signed on from either party, so no partisan split is visible in the record; a Republican senator sponsored the bill to a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.industry: State and local governments and their officials
industries.note: The bill would expose state and local officials to new federal felonies of up to 10 years for defrauding residents of honest services or fair elections, and expose governments to civil liability, including suits where a liable state can demand contribution from the individual employee at fault [S3]. Their exposure arises from defrauding the very residents the bill protects.

The election provisions criminalize, with up to 10-year terms, false ballots, paying for votes, fraudulent registrations, false campaign-finance reports, and voter intimidation — conduct that benefits whoever engages in it at the direct expense of voters [S3].
